body: The book in his hands is the only one open in the room. A man from Sheffield is at the back of a hall on the other side of the world, on the second Sunday of a work posting, and the congregation is singing something he does not recognise. It goes on for three lines before he understands that he does recognise it — that it is the tune he sang at school assembly in 1974, at about half the speed, in a harmony that goes somewhere else at the end of every phrase, with a drum underneath it that was certainly not there in 1974. He finds his place in the book. The book is no use to him whatsoever.

What he is hearing is not a variation on the hymn, or a local flavouring of it. It is the hymn. It simply does not belong to the people who brought it any more, and has not belonged to them for a very long time.

The mission-era arrangement was straightforward enough. The hymnbook arrived, the local music was discouraged or forbidden outright, and congregations were taught European tunes in four parts, usually in translation, frequently alongside instructions about clothing and dancing.

It is worth being exact about what was actually prohibited, because it was rarely the melody. It was the rhythm and the body. Drums were confiscated, dances were stopped, and the correct posture for praise was standing reasonably still and holding a book at chest height. Harmony was permitted; percussion was not. That detail explains the shape of everything that came afterwards, because the rhythm is the element that came back first and came back hardest. A thing that has been taken away is remembered quite differently from a thing that was merely absent, and two generations later the congregations knew precisely which part of their singing had been removed from them.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air today. One of those, HM 311.50, is Riddim and Rhyme, carrying Afro-Caribbean worship — a permanent number for a music that arrived by exactly the route described above.

Keeping a permanent frequency for it is a commitment nobody would make on the numbers. It is a small catalogue by world standards and the people it belongs to are scattered across islands and diaspora congregations with no advertiser in common. It is held because the story it carries is not decoration. The hymn was imposed, learned, kept, and then quietly rebuilt into something the people who imposed it would not recognise, and a dial with no room for that has no room for most of what actually happened to Christian music in the last two centuries.

There are two ready-made accounts of all this and both flatter whoever is telling them. In the first, the gospel arrived and improved the singing, and everything since has been a happy continuation. In the second, the gospel arrived and erased the singing, and everything since has been wreckage. They disagree about the verdict and agree entirely about the plot, which is that something was done to people who had no say in it. That is the part that is wrong, and it is difficult to see from either end of the argument.

What actually happened is audible if you know what to listen for. The tune is kept more or less intact, because the tune is the part that was learned by heart. The harmony is re-voiced, often into parts with nothing to do with the original setting. The tempo goes somewhere else, usually slower and then suddenly not. The rhythm comes back underneath. Call-and-response is reinstated, so a line written to be sung by everybody at once is now thrown and returned. And the book is closed, because nobody in the room needs it.
None of that was a project. There was no committee and no revival of anything. It is what a congregation does to a song it has sung every week for eighty years.

The alternative approach is the purity project, and it deserves a fair hearing, because the loss it responds to is real. Go back behind the missionaries. Recover the old forms, the old instruments, the songs that were suppressed, and set the imported material aside as the residue of somebody else’s power. There is genuine scholarship in that work and genuine grief. But it treats two hundred years as an interruption to be edited out, and the people who lived through them — who sang those hymns at their weddings and over their dead — as having been mistaken about their own lives. It preserves a culture by disqualifying its grandparents.
Nothing survives by being protected from the people who sing it.

A boy of nine is standing between two uncles in a garage after a funeral, in front of a chest freezer with the tea things laid out on top of it. He is singing the bass line, which nobody taught him, because he has heard it every week of his life and there was no point at which he learned it. Around the third verse the tempo drops, without anybody deciding to drop it. One of the uncles starts a rhythm on the side of the freezer with the flat of his hand. The hymn is English and about a hundred and sixty years old, and by the last verse it is not, and the boy notices nothing at all, because nothing has happened. This is how the song goes.
Nobody in that garage was preserving anything. That is the difference between a tradition and an archive: an archive is maintained, and a tradition is used.

Something was genuinely lost, and repossession does not hand it back. Songs went that nobody had written down. Instruments were burned. Dances stopped being danced inside a single generation, with no notation and no recording to work from, and the people who could have said what a particular drum was for died without anybody asking them. No amount of taking the hymn over returns any of that, and it would be dishonest to let a good story about resilience stand in for the missing half of the shelf.

But the choice was never between an inheritance that changed and one that did not. It was between a changed inheritance and none at all. A song that may only be sung the way it was handed over has a shelf life of one generation of obedience; the ones that lasted are the ones that were taken over. What looks from outside like corruption of an original is, from the inside, the only mechanism by which anything survives contact with people. The rebuilding is not damage to the hymn. It is the reason there is still a hymn.

So the honest account is neither of the two on offer. A body of music was imposed on people who did not ask for it, by people who were wrong about a good deal, and those people learned it, and kept it after the supervision ended, and rebuilt it around the one element that had been taken from them. That is not surrender and it is not resistance. It is what possession looks like, and it takes about three generations.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing, so here is the part that is not.

The band carries four kinds of programming: music, which is most of it; teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung; family programming, safe to have on with children in the room; and the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. The music end of the dial is arranged partly by where a sound comes from rather than by what it sells — a Middle Eastern frequency, an Afro-Caribbean one, a Latin one working in two languages at once. It is not a world-music shelf. Each of those is somebody’s ordinary Sunday.

The one to start with is HM 312.10 — Island Hallelujah, carrying Hawaiian praise. It is the cleanest demonstration of everything above. The hymns came ashore in the nineteenth century and were taught in parts out of a book, and what is sung now is those hymns, unmistakably, at a pace the compilers would have thought an error, in harmony that goes where the room decides, with the language back in and the rhythm back underneath. Nothing on that frequency is a reconstruction of what came before the hymnbook. It is what the hymnbook turned into once it belonged to the people singing out of it, which is a different and a considerably better thing to be listening to.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So do not put HM 312.10 on in order to study it, and do not put it on because it is interesting, which it is, and which is not the point. Put it on while the dinner is going or the car is being loaded, and let it run past the point where you have identified the tune. Somewhere in the second half hour a hymn you were taught as a child will arrive from an entirely unexpected direction, and it will still be the hymn. That is what something looks like when it has been kept properly. It has been changed by the keeping.
